02

Device settings

Cycling, timing & adaptation

Patient-triggered breaths flow-cycle between Ti min and Ti max. A higher percentage usually cycles earlier. Timed breaths use fixed Ti or flow cycling within Ti min/max. Rise time sets how quickly pressure rises toward IPAP. A lower flow-trigger threshold is more sensitive. Trigger range: VOCSN-style 0.5–9 L/min in 0.5 L/min increments.

03

The patient

Va needed at the chosen reference CO₂. Changing demand adjusts VCO₂; this is not measured ventilation.

Advanced patient physiology

Semi-sinusoidal Pmus duration is capped at 60% of the patient cycle. Both effort and RR respond to delayed CO₂, without controller smoothing.

Calibrated baseline Pmus:

VCO₂ and reference CO₂ must correspond to required Va within 1–15 L/min. Storage τ is defined at the starting required Va; washout becomes faster at higher ventilation.

Model assumptions, equations & sources

1 · Targets and dead space

V̇E = VT × RR / 1000; V̇A = max(VT − VD, 0) × RR / 1000. A Va target corresponds to VT = 1000 × V̇A / RR + VD. VT and VD are in mL. The top calculator assumes actual RR equals the set backup/target patient rate; the live model measures intervals between ventilator breath starts.

VD = 120 × (height / 175)2.363 mL, as used by the ResMed iVAPS calculator (checked October 13, 2026). Weight-normalized calculated VT: cc/kg IBW = calculated VT (mL) ÷ weight (kg). The chosen IBW convention is ARDSNet predicted body weight: male = 50 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4); female = 45.5 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4). The displayed weight is rounded to one decimal, but the ratio uses the unrounded value. It updates in both VT and Va target modes. The sex formula defaults to male and is selectable beside height. This is not actual body weight; the normalization does not change the simulated mechanics, dead space or controller. Adult formula extrapolation below 152.4 cm is flagged. Source: ARDS Network (2000), Ventilation with lower tidal volumes. Displaying this ratio is not a recommended NIV tidal-volume target.

The dead-space formula above estimates anatomical dead space only. Disease-related physiological dead space, shunt and gas-exchange heterogeneity are not represented.

2 · Coupled respiratory mechanics

Q = [Paw − EPAP − Pmus − V/C] / R; dV/dt = Q. Q is L/s, V is liters above the equilibrium volume at EPAP, C is L/cmH₂O, and R is cmH₂O/(L/s). Inspiratory Pmus is negative, so it adds to inspiratory driving pressure. Airway pressure equals EPAP plus delivered PS, with an adjustable smooth pressure rise (default 150 ms), a fixed 120 ms pressure fall, and flow/time cycling as described below.

A fourth-order Runge–Kutta solver advances every 5 ms. Flow is obtained directly from the equation of motion; volume is integrated and carried across breaths. There is no prescribed VT or artificial flow normalization. Incomplete expiration and residual elastic pressure V/C can therefore occur. The volume trace is not reset each breath; its peak is not necessarily expired VT. EPAP defines the reference equilibrium only; changing it does not model recruitment or changes in resting lung volume.

This is a linear, single-compartment respiratory system with constant R and C per supported breath. See Fresnel, Muir & Letellier (2014) for the equation-of-motion framework and muscle-pressure modeling. We do not implement their proposed muscle waveform.

3 · Semi-sinusoidal Pmus and patient timing

Pmus = −A sin(πs/Tmus) during each patient effort, and zero outside it. A is peak amplitude, s is time since effort onset, and Tmus is the user-set effort duration (default 1.0 s), capped at 60% of the current patient cycle. Amplitude and duration are sampled at effort onset. Pausing effort immediately suppresses Pmus.

The patient has an independent phase clock, advancing at RRpatient/60 cycles per second. A ventilator breath does not reset that clock. Therefore effort can begin before support, persist beyond device cycling, occur without triggering support, or overlap a timed breath. “Timed” identifies the trigger source; it does not imply passive muscles. No reverse-trigger entrainment or detailed neural oscillator is modeled.

Semi-sinusoidal effort is a bench-model convention, not a universal physiological waveform. Beloncle et al. (2016) used semi-sinusoidal effort with configurable rise/release times and also tested a recorded patient signal. Our symmetric half-sine is a simpler choice. Mecklenburgh & Mapleson (1998) found interindividual variation in effort shape and changes in amplitude and duration with assistance.

4 · Metabolism, CO₂ storage and delay

Required Va = 0.863 × VCO₂ / reference PaCO₂, using VCO₂ in mL/min STPD and Va in L/min BTPS. Default VCO₂ is 264.2 mL/min, reference CO₂ 40 mmHg, giving approximately 5.70 L/min required Va. Required Va is displayed to two decimals; editing it adjusts VCO₂. Changing reference CO₂ alone keeps VCO₂ fixed. Height and sex do not estimate metabolism. The height-derived anatomical dead space is also used for patient gas exchange in this version.

Storage mass balance: dP/dt = [0.863 × VCO₂ − P × Va(t)] / [Va₀ × τstorage]. Va₀ is required Va captured at run initialization; τstorage defaults to 60 s. Va(t) is alveolar expiratory volume in the current integration step × 60/dt, after subtracting dead space once per supported-breath interval. The equation is integrated with its exact constant-flow solution over each 5 ms step, including a linear CO₂ rise at zero alveolar outflow. This is a lumped effective storage model, not separate blood/tissue compartments; within-breath CO₂ pulsation is possible.

For constant Va, equilibrium P = 0.863 × VCO₂ / Va and the effective washout time constant is τstorage × Va₀ / Va. Thus the selected τ is defined at initial required Va, rather than forcing the same washout speed at every ventilation. Changing storage τ changes effective capacity; a metabolic, mechanics or reference-CO₂ step does not silently redefine Va₀. There is no extra ventilation filter or controller time constant.

Pure chemoreflex delay: sensed CO₂(t) = model CO₂(t − delay), default 5 s, using interpolation of retained CO₂ history. Zero delay uses current CO₂ directly. Before time zero, CO₂ equals the run’s initial reference value. Increasing delay during a run uses up to 60 seconds of retained history. The controller applies no additional low-pass filter.

The 60-second storage default and the lumped compartments are teaching choices. Khoo et al. (1982) motivate the roles of storage, delay and sensitivity in stability. Human respiratory-control system identification distinguishes plant dynamics from controller dynamics; its fitted coefficients are not directly substituted into this simplified model.

5 · Calibrated eupnea, Pmus and patient rate

Baseline Pmus is computed, not entered. At initialization or Reset, required unassisted VT = required Va / baseline RR + dead space (consistent liter units). The model solves the single-compartment equation of motion over a periodic, unassisted semi-sinusoidal effort cycle with current R, C, baseline RR and effort duration. It first finds periodic residual volume and expired VT for unit effort, then scales amplitude to reach the required expired VT. Linearity makes this a direct numerical calibration; it includes incomplete expiration. Pressure support, backup and device targets do not participate in calibration.

Calibration establishes the unassisted baseline, not the initial supported equilibrium. The supported run starts with zero volume above EPAP equilibrium, CO₂ at reference, and device PS of 12 cmH₂O within the configured limits. Transient adaptation is expected. The baseline Pmus and initial Va₀ remain fixed during all step changes, including changes in mechanics, metabolism and breathing timing. Reset recalibrates with current settings. Restore starting settings preserves calibration, time, history and current physiological state.

Let e = delayed sensed CO₂ − reference CO₂. Peak |Pmus| = clamp[A₀ + Gmus × e, 0, max(30, 3A₀)], in cmH₂O, where A₀ is calibrated baseline amplitude. The upper limit is a numerical teaching bound, not a muscle-strength estimate. RRcommand = clamp[RR₀ + GRR × e, 6, 35] breaths/min. Defaults: RR₀ = 16/min, Gmus = 1 cmH₂O/mmHg, GRR = 0.25 breaths/min/mmHg. Both gains are explicit model assumptions. At reference CO₂, active patient rhythm is 16/min; it is no longer driven directly by observed Va mismatch. Pressure support and mechanics influence rhythm through CO₂.

At positive Pmus gain, the zero-amplitude threshold is reference CO₂ − A₀/Gmus, displayed in the advanced panel. Gain zero removes that CO₂-dependent suppression. Patient rhythm is suppressed if effort amplitude is ≤0.05 cmH₂O or Pause spontaneous effort is enabled. The independent patient phase is not reset by device breaths. Pmus amplitude and duration are sampled at each effort onset; patient rhythm responds to delayed CO₂ each integration step. Observed device RR may differ because of backup, missed triggers or double triggering.

Reference CO₂ defines the operating point, not a guaranteed achieved value. Proportional feedback permits steady offsets. Neither reference CO₂ nor device ventilation targets automatically recalibrate muscle effort. No integral controller, Otis optimization, oxygen feedback, wakefulness drive or controller response τ is included. Sources supporting the modeling framework: Integrated cardiopulmonary model with amplitude and frequency responses; Inspiratory unloading and respiratory motor response to CO₂. These do not validate this simulator’s particular gains or calibration.

6 · Flow cycling, Ti limits and double triggering

During each patient-triggered inspiration, the model tracks the maximum positive inspiratory flow. When current flow falls to or below the selected percentage of that peak, support can cycle to EPAP. Default cycle sensitivity is 25%, with a teaching range of 5–80%. Higher percentages generally shorten device Ti; lower percentages lengthen it. The flow chart shows the current peak-based threshold for each breath in dashed amber.

Ti min (default 0.3 s) blocks flow cycling until that time. If flow is already below threshold when the minimum expires, the breath ends with a “min” marker. Otherwise a subsequent threshold crossing is marked “F”. Ti max (default 2.0 s) forces cycle-off and is marked “max”; it takes priority if thresholds coincide. Equal Ti min and max therefore produce fixed-duration support. Cycling is checked every 5 ms.

Timed breaths: choose Fixed Ti (default) or Flow cycling · Ti min/max. Fixed Ti ends inspiration at the separate timed-breath Ti (default 1.2 s), independently of Ti min/max, and shows “Ti”. Flow cycling uses the same peak-flow threshold and Ti-min/Ti-max rules as patient-triggered breaths, with “F”, “min” or “max” cycle markers. The breath-onset marker remains “T” because backup triggered the breath; cycling mode changes how it ends, not how it starts. Settings are frozen at each supported breath start; edits apply to the next one. There is no automatic rate-based Ti cap; long inspiration can postpone the next backup breath. Actual Ti is measured to the start of pressure fall; the 0.12 s fall is additional. Effort duration remains independent.

References: Hamilton Medical, How to set expiratory trigger sensitivity describes peak-flow cycling and early/late cycling; ResMed TiControl describes the Ti-min/Ti-max window. Hamilton’s mode comparison distinguishes spontaneous flow cycling from mandatory timing. Our numerical thresholds and timed-breath options are explicitly generic, not a reconstruction of iVAPS or every NIV device.

Rise time and flow-trigger sensitivity

Rise time is the duration of the smooth EPAP-to-IPAP ramp: PS × (3u² − 2u³), with u = elapsed inspiration / rise time, limited to 0–1. The selectable teaching range is 50–600 ms in 50 ms increments, default 150 ms. It applies to both patient-triggered and timed breaths. If cycling ends inspiration before the ramp completes, pressure falls from the level actually reached over the fixed 120 ms fall time; IPAP may not be reached. Ti min/max and flow cycling still determine when inspiration ends.

Flow-trigger sensitivity is a threshold of 0.5–9 L/min in 0.5 L/min increments; the simulator default remains 2 L/min. Lower values require less inspiratory flow. It uses net flow into the patient from the equation of motion, requires active patient effort, and respects the existing expiratory lockout. It does not change the timed backup deadline. The numerical flow-trigger range and increment follow React Health VOCSN documentation for active/passive circuits; the 2 L/min default is a simulator choice. The pressure ramp remains an illustrative model. Leak, sensor noise and leak-related auto-triggering are not modeled.

Sources: React Health VOCSN Clinical and Technical Manual, rev. AE (Flow Trigger; software changes); V-Home specifications. ResMed uses qualitative trigger levels from Very Low to Very High (Trigger and Cycle technology); these are not assigned numerical equivalents here. The simulator uses true patient flow without the devices’ leak estimation or proprietary triggering algorithms. Sources checked October 15, 2026.

Triggering and backup

A patient-triggered breath requires an active effort and net inspiratory flow at or above the selected flow-trigger threshold (default 2 L/min), after device inspiration, the 0.12 s pressure fall and a 0.3 s expiratory lockout. A sustained effort can retrigger after that lockout if net inspiratory flow again meets the trigger threshold. D marks a consecutive supported breath associated with the same effort pulse (our operational definition of a same-effort/double trigger); repeat triggering is not imposed and depends on the mechanics and pressure balance. The lockout limits how close breaths can occur. This simplified event definition is not a clinical asynchrony classifier. Auto-PEEP can delay or prevent triggering. Backup starts a timed breath when the interval since the last supported start exceeds 60/active BUR; an eligible patient trigger takes priority. Backup and flow-trigger sensitivity settings apply immediately; pressure, rise time, cycling settings and mechanics apply on the next supported breath. Backup never interrupts an ongoing inspiration or lockout; long Ti can make delivered RR fall below set BUR.

Intelligent BUR starts at two-thirds of the target patient rate. A patient trigger resets it there. Each timed start adds one-twelfth of target rate when last completed-breath Va is below its target, or one-twenty-fourth otherwise, capped at the target rate. Thus escalation takes four or eight timed starts. For VT mode, the Va comparator is the VT equivalent at set BUR. High Va does not disable backup.

This is an explicitly illustrative ramp: ResMed’s Lumis clinical guide, iBR section describes a background of two-thirds, reset after a spontaneous trigger, and fastest escalation in 4–5 breaths below target ventilation. It does not specify our above-target eight-breath rule. Our VT-mode extension and triggering/controller rules are not ResMed algorithms.

After each completed supported interval, PS responds to expired VT error, or Va error converted to a VT error at measured RR. The requested change is (1 − exp[−interval/20 s]) × error / (40 mL/cmH₂O), bounded by the adaptation limit × interval/60 and the PS limits. The default adaptation limit is 5 cmH₂O per simulated minute. Initial PS is 12 cmH₂O within the allowed range. These are illustrative controller choices.

7 · Step-change experiments and display

Open Step changes beside the waveform heading to show the compact scenario panel (collapsed by default). The six scenario buttons change only their named setting, at the time clicked: increase R by 30%, decrease C by 30%, increase required Va by 30%, pause effort, or set the cycle threshold to 50% / 10%. Percentage changes use the current value, so repeated clicks compound. Results are rounded to 0.01 and kept within the control limits; the change caption identifies any limit reached and shows actual before/after values. Other settings, volume, CO₂, controller state and graph history are retained. Consequently outcomes depend on the current state. Clicking an already-matching setting or a percentage scenario already at its limit does not add another event. “Restore last change” reverses the last scenario’s changed fields; repeated use walks backward through scenario changes without clearing history.

Each successful setting change is labeled E1, E2… on the Pmus graph, with a vertical line shared across traces and trends. Closely spaced labels may be omitted visually; full details remain in Recent setting changes. Restore starting settings returns all clinical controls to the settings captured when this run began (on page load or the last Reset / Restore defaults), as a new step change. Elapsed time, graph and event history, volume, CO₂, patient rhythm and adaptive PS are preserved; playback continues if running and remains paused if paused. The scenario restore stack is cleared. Reset and Restore defaults start a new run and clear history.

To explore repeated triggering, try a longer patient effort with early flow cycling or a short Ti max, then inspect whether effort and net inspiratory flow persist after the expiratory lockout. A second breath is not guaranteed. D uses the same-effort event rule above; it may also identify later repeated triggers in a chain. The model has no reverse-trigger entrainment.

Achieved VT is the integral of expiratory flow between consecutive ventilator-breath starts. Va and V̇E are breath-equivalent values from that expired volume and measured interval, not rolling minute measurements. During closely spaced or stacked breaths, interval-based VT, Va and RR can change sharply; dead space is subtracted once per supported interval, so these are simplified estimates during asynchrony. Values remain blank until an interval completes. Device inspiration is shaded; P/T markers identify patient versus timer triggering. Patient rhythm shown in the status line can differ from actual supported RR.

All four waveforms come from the same mechanics simulation. Pmus remains a prescribed shape, but now actually drives flow and volume. No target-volume line is drawn because absolute volume can include residual volume above the EPAP equilibrium. Purple dotted lines mark setting changes.

Playback 1×/2× changes wall-clock speed only. Waveform windows of 15 s, 30 s, 1 min and 2 min use simulated time. All three trend graphs start at time zero and expand with elapsed simulated time (with a 30 s minimum span), independently of the waveform window. Once the run exceeds 5 minutes, they show the latest 300 seconds. Reset or a defaults reset clears the run history. Completed-breath values begin at the first completed interval, with no invented VT, Va or RR value at time zero. The combined VT/RR graph uses expired VT in mL on the left axis and observed ventilator RR in breaths/min on the right; this is not the independent patient rhythm. Both vertical scales adjust to the retained data. The PS band shows the current configured limits. Setting-change markers appear within the displayed trend interval. Pause freezes the model; One breath advances to the next supported breath start. Reset clears history, initializes CO₂ at the selected reference value and recalibrates unassisted baseline Pmus with current settings. Restore defaults (below) restarts the simulation and resets clinical controls to baseline, including BUR 15/min, demand Va 5.70 L/min, resistance 5 cmH₂O/(L/s), compliance 50 mL/cmH₂O and Pmus effort duration 1.0 s.

Adult teaching model; not a device emulator, validated patient model or clinical titration calculator. No leaks, upper-airway obstruction, auto-EPAP, muscle fatigue, nonlinear mechanics or oxygenation. Validate conclusions against clinical evidence rather than treating these simulated values as predictions.
